claim: Grief, voiced in measured lines and repeated, became poetry.

heals.why: grief given a form becomes something made, it need not stay raw

cultivates.why: the poem is born from feeling another creature's loss

commentary.reading: Valmiki's sorrow for the slain crane is read as the seed of the whole poem and of its karuna rasa; shoka itself turned into shloka.
commentary.source: Anandavardhana, Dhvanyaloka 1.5, citing this line; Govindaraja not consulted

claim: Ten years slipped by like one day while I was lost in desire and did not see the obstacle.

depicts.why: he wakes to find a decade gone without noticing
the regret of seeing how far he drifted from his aim

commentary.reading: Vishvamitra recognises the lapse in his tapas and is seized by remorse; the next verses show him sighing with regret and leaving for sterner practice.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Bala Kanda 63 in context; plain sense

claim: Anger destroyed what years of effort earned and left him without peace; he vowed never to act or speak from anger again.

depicts.why: troubled mind after an outburst that cost him his own work

heals.why: shows the cost of anger and the vow that follows it

cultivates.why: he begins again with a specific vow: no anger, no speech in anger

commentary.reading: Vishvamitra's fall through krodha after conquering kama; unmastered senses undo tapas, and he responds with a fresh vow of silence and restraint.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Bala Kanda 64 in context; plain sense

claim: A self-possessed person is satisfied by one kindness and does not store up even a hundred wrongs.

heals.why: grievance is simply not kept on the books

cultivates.why: one kindness is allowed to be enough
wrongs are not rehearsed

commentary.reading: One of Rama's gunas in the opening portrait: because he is atmavan, master of himself, gratitude comes quickly and grievance is not held.
commentary.source: Plain sense in the guna list of Ayodhya 1; commentators' gloss on atmavattaya not checked

claim: A leader should take counsel neither alone nor with too many, and keep a decided plan from leaking.

cultivates.why: a simple rule for how to deliberate and when to stay quiet

commentary.reading: Part of Rama's kaccit questions, royal ethics put as caring enquiry; this one concerns mantra-gupti, guarding counsel.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the kaccit sarga (Ayodhya 100); standard rajaniti reading

claim: I see no fault at all in you, and you should not condemn your mother out of immaturity.

heals.why: the wronged person himself says the shame is not yours to carry
asks him not to turn on his mother

cultivates.why: release of blame toward a parent

commentary.reading: Rama, the one actually wronged, frees Bharata of inherited guilt and asks him not to revile Kaikeyi.
commentary.source: Plain sense in its scene; Govindaraja and Tilaka not consulted for this verse

line_issue: 'Youthful anger' adds anger; balyat means immaturity. Suggested: 'I see no fault in you, not the smallest. And do not condemn your mother out of immaturity.'

claim: The kind words my father spoke when I did well, I will never hear again.

depicts.why: grief lands on one small missing thing, a father's voice of approval
no one is left who speaks to him that way

commentary.reading: Rama's lament on learning of Dasharatha's death; even Rama grieves aloud before he consoles anyone.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 103 in context; plain sense

claim: All that is gathered is spent, all that rises falls, every meeting ends in parting and every life in death.

heals.why: places one loss inside the law that governs everything
what was held was always going to part

cultivates.why: sees parting as built into meeting
sees what lasts and what does not

needs: The reader has already been allowed to grieve; in the first days of a loss it lands cold.

commentary.reading: Rama consoles Bharata after himself weeping and performing the rites: impermanence is the nature of things, so grief should not rule the living. A widely repeated subhashita.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 105 in context; plain sense

claim: As driftwood meets and parts at sea, family and wealth come together and part; their separation is certain.

heals.why: parting is shown as natural and not a failure
togetherness was always for a time

cultivates.why: holding people closely but knowing the time is lent

needs: The reader has already been allowed to grieve.

commentary.reading: Same consolation: meetings are like logs brought together by the current; Rama uses it to steady Bharata, not to belittle love.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 105 in context; plain sense

claim: Conduct alone shows whether a person is noble or base, brave or boastful, pure or impure.

heals.why: worth is measured by what you do, not by birth or others' claims

cultivates.why: self-respect rests on one's own conduct

needs: The reader is not carrying guilt over a past act; then it reads as a verdict.

commentary.reading: Rama's reply to Jabali: if he broke his word his conduct would expose him as ignoble, whatever his birth. Charitra is the test of a person.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 109 in context; plain sense

claim: Kaikeyi demands a binding promise before she will reveal what she wants.

commentary.reading: The setting of the trap: Dasharatha, bound by love and by his word, is made to promise blind.
commentary.source: Plain sense in its scene; Govindaraja and Tilaka not consulted for this verse

line_issue: The line adds an instruction the verse does not give ('Never agree before you know the ask'). Suggested: 'Promise me first, she said. Then I will tell you what I want.' Keep the lesson for the reflection.

claim: Your mother acted for you, from desire or greed; do not hold it in mind, and treat her as a mother.

heals.why: asks him to put down resentment toward a parent

cultivates.why: keep the relationship without excusing the act

commentary.reading: Rama's parting request to Bharata; the wronged one asks that Kaikeyi still be honoured as mother.
commentary.source: Plain sense in its scene; Govindaraja and Tilaka not consulted for this verse

claim: As Rama gave up the earth and left for the forest, no change showed in his mind, like one beyond the world.

cultivates.why: a picture of a mind that loss does not rearrange
the kingdom was held without clinging

commentary.reading: Sarvalokatiga is taken as one gone beyond the world, like a yogi; the poem also shows Rama grieving later, so this is composure, not numbness.
commentary.source: Plain sense; gloss of sarvalokatiga as a liberated person recalled from the Tilaka, not verified

claim: One thing alone burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself.

depicts.why: he accepts the loss, and still the hurt of being bypassed by his own father burns

commentary.reading: Rama accepts exile without protest yet names one hurt: his father's silence. He adds that he would have given Bharata everything unasked.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 19 in context; plain sense

claim: Hold back anger and grief, rely on steadiness, set the insult aside, and get on with what must be done.

heals.why: names the anger and asks for steadiness before any act

cultivates.why: leaning on steadiness alone when insulted

commentary.reading: Rama, who is the injured party, calms Lakshmana's fury on his behalf; it is his own choice of response, not a rule imposed on the wronged.
commentary.source: Plain sense in its scene; Govindaraja and Tilaka not consulted for this verse

claim: Do not leave for the forest without me; hardship, wilderness or heaven, let it be with you.

cultivates.why: a commitment chosen and argued for, not assigned
she insists and wins the argument

commentary.reading: Sita overrules Rama's attempt to leave her behind; the sarga presents her going as her own resolve.
commentary.source: Plain sense in its scene; Govindaraja and Tilaka not consulted for this verse

claim: See Rama as your father, Sita as your mother, the forest as Ayodhya, and go gladly, my son.

heals.why: home is carried in the people you serve and travel with

cultivates.why: treat those in your care as you would your parents

commentary.reading: A mother releases her son by telling him where to find father, mother and home. Govindaraja adds devotional readings (Rama as Vishnu, Sita as Lakshmi); tradition counts it among the finest verses of the poem.
commentary.source: Plain sense; Govindaraja's multiple readings recalled, not verified against the text

claim: Do not sideline your aged father; live as prince by carrying out his word.

cultivates.why: keeping an ageing parent's authority intact in daily decisions
seeing what old age takes from him

commentary.reading: Rama's message through Sumantra: Bharata as yuvaraja should uphold the old king's command and not displace him.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 58 in context; plain sense

line_issue: 'Let him still feel he leads' suggests managing appearances; the verse says to keep carrying out his command. Suggested: 'Your father has grown old. Do not push him aside; keep honouring his word.'

claim: Grief destroys steadiness, learning and everything else; there is no enemy like grief.

depicts.why: spoken by a mother who has just seen what her grief made her say

heals.why: the harsh words were grief speaking, and can be owned and mended

commentary.reading: Kausalya's apology to Dasharatha after reproaching him: she knows dharma, yet grief for her son overturned her judgement.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 62 in context; plain sense

claim: One who begins an act without weighing its gravity, its result and its harm is called a fool.

depicts.why: a dying man tracing his sorrow to one rash act of his youth

commentary.reading: Dasharatha prefaces the story of the hermit boy he killed: karma done without foresight returns; bala here means a fool.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 63 in context; plain sense

claim: My father died while I was away; fortunate are those who could perform his last rites themselves.

depicts.why: loss met at a distance, with no goodbye
the ache of not having been there

commentary.reading: Bharata's first words of grief on returning; he does not yet know Rama was exiled, which sharpens the pathos.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 72 in context; plain sense

claim: Where is my father's gentle hand that used to wipe the dust from me again and again?

depicts.why: grief remembered through a father's touch
the hand that cared for him is gone

commentary.reading: Bharata's lament; karuna rasa through one bodily memory.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 72 in context; plain sense

claim: Wealth that comes through the ruin of kin or friends is to be refused like poisoned food.

heals.why: gain at others' cost is shown as poison

cultivates.why: a clear test for what not to accept
kin and friends weigh more than the prize

commentary.reading: Rama rejects Lakshmana's suspicion of Bharata: he wants artha, kama and even the earth only for his brothers' sake.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 97 in context; plain sense

claim: The earth is not hard for me to win, yet I would not want even Indra's throne through adharma.

heals.why: power is declined when the means are wrong

cultivates.why: strength that chooses not to take
the means decide whether a prize is worth having

commentary.reading: Rama states capability and restraint together: he could take the kingdom and will not, because it would be adharma.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 97 in context; plain sense

claim: You spoke from love and friendship; no one counsels a person they do not care for.

heals.why: a loved one's objection is read as care, which cools the defensive reply

cultivates.why: thanking the person who questions you
hearing counsel as friendship

commentary.reading: Rama thanks Sita for questioning his vow, then still keeps it: counsel is honoured and the decision remains his.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Aranya 10 in context; plain sense

claim: No jewelled deer like this exists on earth; its form is certainly a trick of illusion.

heals.why: names the glitter as a made thing before anyone chases it
the wanting is checked by asking whether the object is even real

cultivates.why: testing an attraction against what actually exists

commentary.reading: Lakshmana recognises Maricha's maya. Rama hears him and still goes, reasoning that a real deer is a prize and a demon should be killed; the warning is sound and unheeded.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Aranya 43 in context; plain sense

claim: Take up only the burden that will not break you, and eat only what you can digest without harm.

heals.why: overreach is named as the thing that destroys the one who grasps

cultivates.why: measuring a load before lifting it

commentary.reading: Jatayu's warning to Ravana: seizing Sita is a load that will crush him. A general maxim (nyaya) used as a rebuke to a wrongdoer, not as gentle advice on workload.
commentary.source: Plain sense in its scene; Govindaraja and Tilaka not consulted for this verse

claim: You should not destroy the worlds for the offence of one being.

heals.why: keeps rage from spilling onto those who did nothing

cultivates.why: find who actually did this before acting
the innocent are kept in view

commentary.reading: Lakshmana does not ask Rama to forgive; he asks him to aim his anger: trace the abductor, try fair means first, and use force if Sita is not returned.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Aranya 65 in context; plain sense

claim: Take heart: trouble touches every living being, like fire, and passes in a moment.

heals.why: sorrow is shown as common to all and not a mark against him
a brother's voice saying take heart

cultivates.why: holding on because trouble moves through

commentary.reading: Lakshmana's consolation of Rama, with examples of the great who also suffered; the aim is to restore Rama's own clarity so he can search.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Aranya 66 in context; plain sense

claim: Dharma is won by the skilful through effortful self-discipline; happiness does not come from ease.

heals.why: comfort is shown as a dead end

cultivates.why: choosing discipline as the road
staying with chosen restraints

commentary.reading: Sita's counsel in the forest: dharma is the source of wealth and happiness, and it is reached by patient niyama, not by comfort.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Aranya 9 in context; plain sense

claim: Resolute energy is the greatest strength; nothing is out of reach for one who has it.

heals.why: answers collapse with the one power still in his hands

cultivates.why: names energy of effort as strength itself

commentary.reading: Lakshmana rouses Rama from lament at Pampa: give up grief, hold to steadiness, and effort will recover Sita.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 1 in context; plain sense

line_issue: 'Enthusiasm' reads as cheerfulness; utsaha is resolute energy and perseverance. Suggested: 'There is no strength greater than a spirit that keeps trying. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.'

claim: Your younger brother deserves your affection; near or far he is your kin, and no kinsman equals him.

heals.why: recalls what a brother is beneath the quarrel
asks for a pause before the fight

cultivates.why: seeing the rival as kin again

commentary.reading: Tara counsels Vali, the stronger brother who drove Sugriva out, to reconcile. He ignores her and dies; good counsel refused.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 15 in context; plain sense

claim: Drop this flood of anger the way you cast off last night's garland on rising.

heals.why: an image for putting anger down as something already used up

cultivates.why: letting the surge pass before acting

commentary.reading: Tara stops Vali at the door; anger arriving like a river in spate is to be set aside before deciding.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 15 in context; plain sense

claim: Be neither too familiar nor too distant; both are grave faults, so keep to the middle.

cultivates.why: reading how close to stand with people who hold power over you

commentary.reading: Dying Vali teaches Angada how to live at his uncle's court: measured closeness, attention to place and time.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 22 in context; plain sense

claim: We were not given brotherly love and happiness together; it turned out otherwise.

depicts.why: a dying man looks at the bond with his brother that rivalry cost him
regret that it went wrong between them

commentary.reading: Vali, dying, speaks to Sugriva without rancour and entrusts Angada and Tara to him; he lays the rift on what was ordained.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 22 in context; plain sense

claim: The rains have come; wait for autumn, and then you will defeat Ravana.

heals.why: the urge to act now is given a season to wait for

cultivates.why: waiting as part of the campaign, not a retreat from it

commentary.reading: Lakshmana does not ask Rama to give up the fight; he asks him to wait for the season when action can succeed.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 27 in context; plain sense

claim: His speech was not wordy, unclear, hurried or strained, and came in an even, middle tone.

cultivates.why: a concrete picture of clear, unhurried speech

commentary.reading: Rama's praise of Hanuman's first address: learning shows in speech that is brief, unambiguous and well pitched.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 3 in context; plain sense

claim: You should bear the harsh words of Rama, who is in pain and has lost his wife.

heals.why: hears harshness as pain speaking

cultivates.why: bearing a hurting person's words
remembering what he has lost

commentary.reading: Hanuman tells Sugriva plainly that he is the one at fault for letting his promise slide, so he must bear Rama's anger and make amends.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 32 in context; plain sense

claim: A friend is easily made but hard to keep; minds are changeable and affection breaks over little.

depicts.why: he worries aloud that a small lapse has cost him a friend

commentary.reading: Sugriva, alarmed at Lakshmana's anger, reflects on how friendships must be kept up; Hanuman then shows him the lapse was his own.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 32 in context; plain sense

claim: This is no time for anger, least of all at your own; bear the lapse of one who wishes you well.

heals.why: separates a well-wisher's lapse from an enemy's act

cultivates.why: making room for the failure of someone on your side

commentary.reading: Tara meets Lakshmana's fury with calm reasoning: Sugriva has lapsed, not betrayed.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 33 in context; plain sense

claim: People of real character do not fall under anger's control suddenly, without first reflecting.

heals.why: appeals to his own character instead of scolding

cultivates.why: reflection placed before reaction

commentary.reading: Tara appeals to Lakshmana's sattva: a person of substance examines before yielding to rosha.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 35 in context; plain sense

claim: Those who keep acting surely see the fruit of their action, so weariness is no reason to stop now.

heals.why: meets the weariness of a failing search with the certainty that effort bears fruit

cultivates.why: one more round of effort
not closing one's eyes when tired

commentary.reading: Angada rallies the exhausted search party: put despondency aside and search again. The second half, as usually read, says it does not befit us to shut our eyes now.
commentary.source: Plain sense; the reading 'alam nirvedam agamya na hi no milanam kshamam' is recalled from the vulgate, not verified in the corpus

line_issue: The line and translation turn encouragement into a threat ('sink into despair and you cannot rise'). The verse more likely says that giving up now is not fitting. Suggested: 'Those who keep working do see the fruit of their work. We are worn out, but this is not the time to close our eyes.' Check the Sanskrit reading first.

claim: Your strength, intelligence, energy and courage surpass all beings; why do you not ready yourself?

heals.why: an elder names the capacities he has forgotten
the question turns hesitation into readiness

cultivates.why: remembering one's own strength
the rise that follows being reminded

commentary.reading: Jambavan rouses the silent Hanuman, who had forgotten his powers, by recounting his birth and strength; Hanuman then grows for the leap.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 66 in context; plain sense

claim: In calamity, loss of wealth or mortal fear, the steady person who reflects with their own mind does not sink.

heals.why: steadiness plus one's own thinking keeps a person afloat
even mortal fear is listed as something one can think through

cultivates.why: the quality that does not go under
using one's own judgement in crisis

commentary.reading: Sugriva, who has lost wife and kingdom himself, steadies Rama: the dhritiman does not collapse; grief only drains strength.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 7 in context; plain sense

claim: One who has steadiness, foresight, judgement and skill does not sink in any task.

cultivates.why: named first among the four that carry a task
foresight and judgement as working tools

commentary.reading: Praise of Hanuman after he outwits Surasa and Simhika: dhriti, drishti, mati and dakshya are what bring work through.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 1 in context; plain sense

claim: My task's hour is pressing and the day is passing; I have given my word not to stop midway.

heals.why: a pleasant pause is declined because it would break the vow

cultivates.why: the promise decides, not the comfort on offer
keeping to the task while the day lasts

commentary.reading: Hanuman honours Mainaka's hospitality by touching the mountain with his hand and flies on; courtesy kept, vow kept.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 1 in context; plain sense

claim: Not losing heart is the root of fortune and the highest happiness; I will search again where I have not searched.

heals.why: he answers his own collapse with a principle and a next step
weariness is refused a verdict

cultivates.why: perseverance named as the root of success
a concrete plan: the places not yet searched

commentary.reading: Hanuman's self-counsel after searching Lanka in vain: anirveda makes a creature's work fruitful, so he resumes the search.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 12 in context; plain sense

claim: I must speak plain human words that carry meaning; otherwise she cannot be comforted.

cultivates.why: he plans his words around her fear, not his own skill
choosing the form of speech the listener can trust

commentary.reading: Hanuman reasons that polished Sanskrit would make Sita take him for Ravana in disguise, so he chooses ordinary human speech and begins by singing of Rama.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 30 in context; plain sense

claim: The old saying is true: joy comes to a person who stays alive, even after a hundred years.

heals.why: spoken by someone who nearly gave up and lived to hear good news
long sorrow is shown as able to end

cultivates.why: trust that joy can return if one stays
staying alive as the one thing asked

commentary.reading: Sita, who had been ready to end her life the night before, hears of Rama and quotes the folk gatha. Bharata repeats it when Rama returns. A protective line for a reader in despair.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 34 in context; plain sense

claim: Fortunate are the great souls who check rising anger with reason, as water puts out fire.

depicts.why: he praises those who hold their temper because he has just failed to

heals.why: reason is named as the water for this fire

cultivates.why: buddhi set against anger at the moment it rises

commentary.reading: Hanuman's remorse after burning Lanka, fearing Sita was harmed; he reasons his way through and learns she is safe.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 55 in context; plain sense

claim: It weighs on me that, poor as I am here, I cannot repay the one who brought me this good news.

depicts.why: he feels the smallness of having nothing to give

cultivates.why: gratitude that wants to repay and cannot

commentary.reading: Rama praises Hanuman's feat and grieves that in exile he has no fitting gift; in the next verse he gives an embrace as his all.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 1 in context; plain sense

line_issue: 'So I'll give what I have: a hug' imports the next verse and is too casual. Suggested: 'It weighs on me that, with nothing of my own here, I cannot repay the one who brought me this news.'

claim: When I was grief-stricken, heedless and despairing in the forests, you were the one who consoled me.

depicts.why: at his brother's side he remembers who held him up through every low hour

cultivates.why: naming what someone has been to you while they can still be told

commentary.reading: Rama's lament over Lakshmana struck by Ravana's spear; he recalls Lakshmana as his samashvasayita, the one who consoled him. Lakshmana recovers.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 101 in context; plain sense

claim: You conquered the worlds by first conquering your senses, and those same senses have now conquered you.

heals.why: shows how the master of the world fell by what he stopped guarding

commentary.reading: Mandodari's lament names the true cause of Ravana's fall: not Rama's arrows first, but his own unguarded senses.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 111 in context; plain sense

claim: The noble do not return evil for evil and show compassion even to the guilty, for no one is without fault.

heals.why: revenge is declined from a position of strength
anger at tormentors is met with a higher standard

cultivates.why: compassion offered even where punishment is deserved
no one is without fault

commentary.reading: Sita, now free and with power to punish, spares the guards who acted on Ravana's orders. Cherished in the Srivaishnava tradition as the mark of her compassion.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 113 in context; the Srivaishnava emphasis is recalled, Govindaraja's gloss not checked

claim: I do not refuse you, but my mind hurries to see my brother Bharata, whose plea I once turned down.

depicts.why: after years away the heart runs ahead to one person at home

commentary.reading: Rama declines Vibhishana's hospitality in Lanka; his thoughts are on Bharata waiting at Nandigrama.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 121 in context; plain sense

claim: If Bharata, after holding it so long, wants the kingdom himself, let him rule the whole earth.

heals.why: even a rightful claim is held loosely

cultivates.why: willing to let the kingdom go if his brother wants it
the brother's wish is placed before the claim

commentary.reading: Rama sends Hanuman ahead to read Bharata's face before assuming anything; Bharata hands everything back. Generosity together with checking the facts.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 125 in context; plain sense

line_issue: 'I won't fight family for it' is not in the verse and reads as advice to give up a rightful claim. Suggested: 'If, after holding it so long, my brother wants the kingdom for himself, let him rule it all.'

claim: I return the kingdom you left in my trust; today my life is fulfilled, seeing you back as king.

cultivates.why: power held as a trust and handed back whole
fulfilment in the other's return, not in keeping

commentary.reading: Bharata completes fourteen years of trusteeship by returning the kingdom as a nyasa, a deposit.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 127 in context; plain sense

claim: Pleasant speakers are always easy to find; one who speaks or hears an unwelcome but wholesome truth is rare.

depicts.why: spoken by a brother just insulted for honest counsel

heals.why: being unheard for honesty is common and does not make the counsel wrong

cultivates.why: the worth of saying the hard, helpful thing

commentary.reading: Vibhishana's parting words to Ravana; the same maxim is spoken by Maricha to Ravana in the Aranya Kanda. Hita that is apriya is the true friend's speech.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 16 in context; plain sense

claim: Forgive what I said for your good; guard yourself and this city; I am leaving, be happy without me.

depicts.why: he leaves hurt and still wishes his brother well

cultivates.why: walking away with dignity after counsel is refused
no curse, only a blessing at the door

commentary.reading: Vibhishana leaves only after repeated counsel is met with public insult; he goes without rancour and seeks Rama's shelter.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 16 in context; plain sense

claim: To anyone who comes even once saying 'I am yours', I give freedom from fear of all beings; this is my vow.

heals.why: shelter is promised without conditions or a second asking

cultivates.why: fearlessness given as a vow
one act of saying 'I am yours' is enough
the promise rests on his vow, not on the seeker's merit

commentary.reading: Rama's abhaya-pradana on accepting Vibhishana against his allies' doubts; the Srivaishnava tradition treats it as a charama shloka, the Lord's own promise of refuge.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 18; Srivaishnava reading (Govindaraja among others) recalled, wording not verified

claim: One in power who does later tasks first and first tasks last does not know good policy from bad.

cultivates.why: sequence is part of judgement

commentary.reading: Kumbhakarna's blunt niti to Ravana: counsel should have come before the abduction, not after. He then fights for his brother all the same.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 63 in context; plain sense

claim: The truly brave cannot bear to praise themselves; without display they do what is hard.

heals.why: self-praise is marked as unworthy of real courage

cultivates.why: courage shown in the deed and not in the telling

commentary.reading: Kumbhakarna's answer to Mahodara's boasting before he goes out to battle.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 65 in context; plain sense

claim: Overcome by grief for the bird, what is this that I have said?

depicts.why: he stops in the middle of his own outburst and questions it

cultivates.why: looking back at one's words while the feeling is still hot

commentary.reading: Valmiki reflects on having cursed the hunter out of grief, and then notices the utterance fell into metre; the reflection opens into the birth of the shloka.
commentary.source: Plain sense; whether the chinta is regret at the curse or wonder at the metre is read both ways, commentaries not checked

claim: Vishvamitra could subdue them himself; he asks for your son for your son's own good.

heals.why: a parent's fear is answered by showing who benefits
holding on is seen as holding back

cultivates.why: trust in a proven teacher

commentary.reading: Vasishtha persuades Dasharatha: the sage does not need Rama's help; Rama needs what the sage will give him.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Bala 21 in context; plain sense

claim: Forbearance is giving, truth, sacrifice, fame and dharma; the world rests on forbearance.

heals.why: restraint from retaliation is held up as the highest strength

cultivates.why: forbearance praised as the ground of every virtue

commentary.reading: Kushanabha praises his daughters, who refused Vayu's advances and were harmed by him, for not cursing him in return. Praise of women's forbearance after an assault needs great care.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Bala 33 in context; plain sense

claim: You have fulfilled the vow your forefathers could not, and have won the highest honour in the world.

cultivates.why: a vow carried across generations and completed
long effort is seen and blessed

commentary.reading: Brahma blesses Bhagiratha, who brought down the Ganga where Sagara, Amshuman and Dilipa could not.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Bala 44 in context; plain sense

line_issue: The line carries the scene and an added moral ('Effort carried forward is not wasted'); the verse itself only says the vow is fulfilled and honour won. Suggested: 'You have carried through the vow that those before you could not. The highest honour is yours.'

claim: Not for a hundred thousand cows or heaps of silver will I give up Shabala; she stays with me.

cultivates.why: a plain no to someone far more powerful
what sustains his life is not for sale

commentary.reading: Vasishtha refuses King Vishvamitra's rising offers for the cow that sustains his rites; the king then tries force and fails.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Bala 53 in context; plain sense

claim: After a thousand years he stood like wood; many obstacles shook him, yet anger found no way in.

heals.why: the same man who lost everything to temper is shown unshaken

cultivates.why: provocation comes and finds no entry
stillness won after relapse

commentary.reading: The end of Vishvamitra's arc: after falling to desire and anger he keeps his vow, and is then acknowledged a brahmarshi.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Bala 65 in context; plain sense

claim: Sita was dear as the wife his father chose, and his love grew further through her qualities; she held him doubly dear.

cultivates.why: affection that deepens through knowing each other's qualities

commentary.reading: The close of the Bala Kanda: a marriage that began by the elders' choice and grew by mutual virtue; their hearts spoke to each other.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Bala 77 in context; plain sense

claim: Always calm within, he spoke gently first and did not answer harsh words in kind.

heals.why: a harsh word is simply not returned

cultivates.why: inner calm shown as a habit of speech
strength that does not need the last word

commentary.reading: From the portrait of Rama's qualities: prashantatma, gentle in address, not retorting to harshness.
commentary.source: Plain sense in the guna list of Ayodhya 1

claim: Once a task of small cost and great yield is decided, begin it quickly and do not delay.

heals.why: delay after deciding is named as the fault

cultivates.why: start at once what is clearly worth doing

commentary.reading: From the kaccit questions: prompt beginning of well-judged work, without dirgha-sutrata, dragging things out.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the kaccit sarga (Ayodhya 100)

claim: One wise person is to be preferred to a thousand fools, for in a crisis the wise bring great good.

cultivates.why: choosing whose advice to keep close

commentary.reading: From the kaccit questions: the value of one learned minister in hard times.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the kaccit sarga (Ayodhya 100)

claim: People rejoice at each sunrise and sunset and do not notice their own life wearing away.

heals.why: the passing of days is made visible

cultivates.why: seeing time as life being spent
less clinging to the day's small gains

commentary.reading: Part of Rama's consolation of Bharata: since life itself is running out for everyone, grieve for yourself and act well, more than for the departed.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 105 in context; plain sense

claim: As rulers conduct themselves, so do the people; if I live by desire, the whole world will follow.

cultivates.why: one's conduct is copied by those who look up to one

commentary.reading: Rama's second reason for refusing Jabali: a king's conduct sets the people's; breaking truth for gain would teach the world to do the same.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 109 in context; plain sense

claim: My brother placed this trust in me out of affection; I will guard it until he returns.

cultivates.why: work held as a trust for someone else
a fourteen-year commitment stated simply

commentary.reading: Bharata at Nandigrama rules as trustee with Rama's sandals on the throne; power as nyasa.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 115 in context; plain sense

claim: Do not anguish over this reversal of fortune; between kingdom and forest, the forest is the greater gain.

heals.why: the lost prize is weighed again and found not to be the only good

cultivates.why: kingdom and forest are held on one scale

commentary.reading: Rama, himself the one dispossessed, tells Lakshmana that the reversal is no cause for torment; he calls forest life mahodaya, of great good.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 22 in context; plain sense

claim: One able to push back fate with effort does not sink when fate damages his aims.

heals.why: a setback called fate is treated as something effort can answer

cultivates.why: paurusha set against daiva
refusing to be told that nothing can be done

commentary.reading: Lakshmana, angry on Rama's behalf, argues that only the weak lean on daiva. Rama respects the spirit and still chooses to keep his father's word; take the teaching on effort, not the urge to fight.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 23 in context; plain sense

claim: Take watchful care that the old king is not worn down or destroyed by grief for his son.

cultivates.why: attentive care for a grieving elder
seeing the father's sorrow even while leaving

commentary.reading: Rama asks Kausalya to stay and tend Dasharatha. The surrounding sarga frames this as a wife's duty to her husband, so use only the care for a grieving elder, with the scene.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 24 in context; plain sense

claim: The hardships of forest life you list are blessings to me, because your love goes before me.

cultivates.why: she has weighed every hardship and still chooses
hardship shared is seen as gain

commentary.reading: Sita answers Rama's list of forest dangers point by point; her going is her own argued decision.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 29 in context; plain sense

claim: Stay this one night where your mother and I can see you; leave tomorrow morning.

depicts.why: a father who cannot stop the leaving asks for one more night
the separation is already felt before it begins

commentary.reading: Dasharatha, bound by his word, pleads for a night; Rama gently declines because the vow is to leave that day.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 34 in context; plain sense

claim: You will see him return from the forest; give up grief and confusion, I tell you truly.

heals.why: a companion's firm assurance that this separation ends
worry for an absent child is answered with his strength and return

cultivates.why: trust in a child's ability to come through

commentary.reading: Sumitra sits with the weeping Kausalya and reasons from Rama's virtues to his safe return.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 44 in context; plain sense

claim: A prince should free the people from suffering caused on his account and never bind them to his own sorrow.

cultivates.why: noticing what one's trouble costs those who follow
a leader carries his own hardship

commentary.reading: Rama slips away at night so the citizens sleeping in the open for his sake will go home. Atmakrita is best taken as suffering caused by the prince himself.
commentary.source: Plain sense in context (Ayodhya 46); the library translation takes atmakrita as the citizens' own doing, which the scene does not support

claim: Give up pride and self-regard among my mothers, and see that Kaikeyi is honoured as the king honours her.

heals.why: asks that a feud at home not be fed

cultivates.why: courtesy kept toward the one who caused the hurt

commentary.reading: Rama's message to his mother from exile: keep the household whole. It asks the wronged senior queen to defer to the co-wife who wronged her.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 58 in context; plain sense

claim: I know dharma and I know you are truthful; what I said, I said in anguish for my son.

depicts.why: she owns the harsh words she spoke
the grief behind them is named plainly

heals.why: an apology that neither excuses nor drowns in blame

commentary.reading: Kausalya asks Dasharatha's pardon with folded hands after her reproach; grief had overturned what she knows.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 62 in context; plain sense

claim: This sorrow has come to me by my own doing, like poison a child eats in ignorance.

depicts.why: he traces his present pain to his own old act
the sorrow is felt as earned

commentary.reading: Dasharatha owns the killing of the hermit boy as the seed of his grief; the simile of the unknowing child keeps it an act of ignorance, not malice.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 63 in context; plain sense

claim: Had you not confessed this evil deed yourself, your head would have burst into a hundred thousand pieces.

cultivates.why: owning a wrong oneself before being found out

commentary.reading: The hermit father tells Dasharatha that his own confession saved him from instant ruin; he is still cursed to die grieving for a son.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 64 in context; plain sense

line_issue: 'You were spared' overstates: he escapes instant death and is still cursed. Suggested: 'Because you came and told us yourself, the worst did not fall on you at once.'

claim: You are our refuge and our eyes; our lives rest on you; why do you not speak?

depicts.why: old parents call to the child their lives depend on, and no answer comes

commentary.reading: The blind father speaks to footsteps he takes for his son's; the son is dead. Among the most painful moments of the Ayodhya Kanda.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 64 in context; plain sense

claim: I see no difference between Rama and Bharata, so I am glad the king will crown Rama.

heals.why: shows the heart before comparison was fed

cultivates.why: gladness at another's rise

commentary.reading: Kaikeyi's first response to the news is joy; she even rewards Manthara. Envy is then talked into her.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 7 in context; plain sense

claim: Why do you blame me, who knew nothing and am without fault? You know how deep my love for Rama is.

depicts.why: falsely accused by someone he loves, for something done in his name

commentary.reading: Bharata answers Kausalya's bitter words and swears his innocence; she then takes him in her arms.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 75 in context; plain sense

claim: Three pairs come to all beings alike and cannot be avoided, so you should not collapse like this.

heals.why: the mourner is placed among all creatures, not singled out
collapse is met with an elder's hand

cultivates.why: standing up again in the face of what cannot be avoided

needs: A mourner who has already wept and now needs help to stand.

commentary.reading: Vasishtha lifts Bharata at the pyre. The three pairs are glossed as hunger and thirst, grief and delusion, old age and death; the verse itself does not list them.
commentary.source: Plain sense; the listing of the pairs follows a traditional gloss recalled, not verified in Govindaraja or the Tilaka

claim: How could a son of Dasharatha usurp a kingdom? The kingdom and I both belong to Rama.

heals.why: a prize arranged by a parent is refused in public

cultivates.why: saying no before the whole assembly
knowing what is not his to take

commentary.reading: Bharata refuses the throne his mother schemed for and resolves to bring Rama back; when Rama will not return, he rules as trustee.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 82 in context; plain sense

claim: If Bharata is well disposed toward Rama, this army will cross the Ganga safely today.

heals.why: suspicion is held open until intent is known

cultivates.why: prepare, then test the facts before judging

commentary.reading: Guha readies his men against a possible threat to Rama and makes passage conditional on Bharata's intent; he then meets him and learns the truth.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 84 in context; plain sense

line_issue: The line is a moral drawn from the scene; the verse is a condition. Suggested: 'If he comes in good faith toward Rama, his army will cross the river safely today.'

claim: When has Bharata ever wronged you, that you now fear and suspect him?

heals.why: suspicion is tested against the person's actual record
fear running ahead of the facts is called back

cultivates.why: trust built on how someone has always behaved

commentary.reading: Rama checks Lakshmana's assumption of the worst; Bharata arrives in grief, not in arms.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 97 in context; plain sense

claim: Those whose time has run out do not accept the good advice their friends give.

depicts.why: an adviser who knows he will not be heard

commentary.reading: Maricha's last plea to Ravana; he then goes along, choosing death at Rama's hands over death at Ravana's.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Aranya 41 in context; plain sense

claim: I am old and you are young and armed, yet you will not carry Vaidehi off unharmed.

heals.why: the odds are stated honestly and he stands anyway

cultivates.why: courage that does not depend on being the stronger
age and weakness do not decide the duty

commentary.reading: Jatayu fights and falls; Rama later performs his last rites as for a father. The stand is honoured though it fails.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Aranya 50 in context; plain sense

claim: You must make Sugriva your friend; I see no success for you without doing so.

heals.why: the way out of loss is shown to run through another person

cultivates.why: seeking out someone who has known the same loss

commentary.reading: Kabandha directs the grieving Rama to Sugriva, who has likewise lost wife and kingdom; friendship sworn before fire follows.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Aranya 72 in context; plain sense

claim: As the great ones told me, I have gathered forest food of many kinds from Pampa's banks for you.

cultivates.why: years of waiting on a teacher's word
the waiting was spent preparing an offering
her whole practice points to this meeting

commentary.reading: Shabari, an ascetic who served Matanga's disciples, receives Rama as her gurus foretold and then ascends. Valmiki does not mention tasted berries.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Aranya 74 in context; plain sense

claim: Keeping weapons close changes the mind, as nearness to fire changes what it touches.

cultivates.why: what you keep at hand slowly shapes what you do

commentary.reading: Sita's parable of the ascetic given a sword to guard, whose mind turned cruel through constant handling of it; she asks Rama not to kill without cause.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Aranya 9 in context; plain sense

claim: Seeing me distressed, the citizens and ministers crowned me; it was not my wish, so please forgive me.

depicts.why: pleading to be believed by someone who has already decided

commentary.reading: Sugriva recounts how he explained and bowed to Vali, who refused to hear him, took his wife and drove him out.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 10 in context; plain sense

claim: Your monkey nature shows: with so flighty a mind you cannot settle yourself in clear judgement.

heals.why: names the jumping mind as the reason no clear thought forms
fear is shown running ahead of the facts

commentary.reading: Hanuman chides Sugriva's panic at the sight of Rama and Lakshmana and advises judging by signs and conduct before fearing.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 2 in context; plain sense

claim: Do not hold my offence against me; I was dragged along by a fated confusion of mind.

depicts.why: at the end he asks not to be remembered by his wrong
he says his judgement was not his own when he did it

commentary.reading: Dying Vali asks Sugriva's pardon and then gives him the golden garland, Angada and Tara to care for. The plea leans on fate; the acts that follow show real amends.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 22 in context; plain sense

claim: How could any brother, even one led by desire, be glad of a brother's death once he weighs kingdom against this grief?

depicts.why: he got what he wanted at a cost he cannot bear
the brother he fought is the brother he mourns

commentary.reading: Sugriva's remorse over Vali's body; he speaks of entering the fire, and Rama and the others steady him.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 24 in context; plain sense

line_issue: The line turns remorse into an instruction ('Weigh the prize... No win is worth a brother'). Suggested: 'How could any brother be glad of this, once he weighs a kingdom against such grief?'

claim: Enough of this anguish; you should not grieve, for every aim of one who keeps grieving falls away.

heals.why: sorrow is shown to be costing him the very thing he wants

cultivates.why: holding purpose through a season of waiting

commentary.reading: Lakshmana to the sleepless Rama in the rains: Sita is alive and can be won back, so grief must not be allowed to eat his strength.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 27 in context; plain sense

claim: Sugriva, once rested, will himself know the time has come and remember the help he received.

heals.why: impatience with a slow friend is held back by trust

cultivates.why: giving a friend time before judging him
expecting the best of someone who owes you

commentary.reading: Rama waits through the rains. When autumn comes and Sugriva still delays, he sends Lakshmana with a stern warning: patience first, then firmness.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 28 and 30 in context; plain sense

claim: One who acts on a friend's need after its time has passed does not serve the friend, however great the deed.

heals.why: comfort is shown to be costing a friend his hour of need

cultivates.why: friendship measured by timeliness

commentary.reading: Hanuman's reminder to Sugriva, lost in pleasure after his coronation, that help to Rama is already overdue.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 29 in context; plain sense

claim: Forgive me, friend, for the harsh words I spoke after hearing the grieving Rama.

depicts.why: he names his own harshness without being asked

heals.why: a short apology that states the words and their cause

cultivates.why: the friendship is put back before the work resumes

commentary.reading: Lakshmana, calmed by Tara and by Sugriva's humility, asks pardon in turn; both sides own their part.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 36 in context; plain sense

claim: I could restore your wings today, but by staying here you will do a work for the good of the world.

heals.why: a life that feels finished is told it still has a task
being grounded is not being useless

cultivates.why: living on through a long wait
trust that the waiting has a purpose

commentary.reading: Sampati, wingless and wanting to die, is told by the sage Nishakara to wait: he will point the monkeys to Sita, and his wings will return. They do.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 62 and 63 in context; plain sense

claim: I am old now and my strength has waned; this is your hour, and you have every quality it needs.

heals.why: an elder says plainly that the moment is his

cultivates.why: being handed the task with full confidence
his qualities are named by someone who knows

commentary.reading: Jambavan recalls his own lost prowess and hands the leap to Hanuman.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 66 in context; plain sense

claim: The foolish person who always yields to helplessness sinks powerless in grief, like an overloaded boat.

cultivates.why: warns what happens when steadiness is given up

commentary.reading: The counterpart to the previous verse on the steady person; Sugriva softens it at once by saying he speaks as a friend, not a teacher.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 7 in context; plain sense

claim: I speak for your good as a friend, not to instruct you; honouring our friendship, do not grieve.

heals.why: comfort offered as friendship, not correction
someone who knows the same loss is beside him

cultivates.why: how to stand by a grieving friend

commentary.reading: Rama wipes his tears, embraces Sugriva and says he has come back to himself; the friend's tone does what the argument alone could not.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 7 in context; plain sense

claim: Rich or poor, happy or unhappy, faultless or flawed, a friend is the highest refuge.

heals.why: a friend is named as refuge in every condition

cultivates.why: friendship that does not depend on fortune or flawlessness
valuing the friends one has

commentary.reading: Sugriva on what friendship is, just after the two have sworn it before the fire.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Kishkindha 8 in context; plain sense

claim: Now that this task is before you, let the ocean and me do you a kindness; please accept it gladly.

cultivates.why: an old kindness is remembered and returned

commentary.reading: Mainaka rises from the sea to repay Vayu's old protection of him; returning a kindness is called the eternal dharma in the adjoining verse.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 1 in context; plain sense

claim: Self-destruction has many faults and the living find good, so I will hold on to life; reunion awaits the living.

depicts.why: he has just weighed ending it all and speaks from that edge

heals.why: the choice to live is made with a reason he can hold
staying is tied to a good still possible

cultivates.why: holding on to life itself
I will keep the breath in this body

commentary.reading: The turn in Hanuman's despair: having thought of fasting to death or fire, he reasons that death would ruin Rama's cause and that the living meet good again. The library line generalises 'self-destruction' to 'giving up'.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 13 in context; plain sense

claim: I cannot be tempted with power or wealth; I am inseparable from Raghava as light is from the sun.

heals.why: a captive answers her captor without bargaining

cultivates.why: a no that offers nothing to negotiate
her loyalty stated as part of what she is

commentary.reading: Sita, placing a blade of grass between herself and Ravana, refuses him. Devotional readers also hear the soul's inseparability from the Lord in ananya.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 21 in context; the devotional reading is recalled, not verified in Govindaraja

claim: Out of sight, affection fades only among the ungrateful; Rama will not let it fade.

depicts.why: alone and far away, she voices the fear of being forgotten
the doubt whether love survives absence

heals.why: she answers the fear from what she knows of him

cultivates.why: trust in the other's constancy

commentary.reading: Sita's lament in the Ashoka grove; she doubts, then recalls Rama's character and holds to it.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 26 in context; plain sense

claim: Battles are uncertain and I dislike a gamble; what wise person would do a sure task in a doubtful way?

cultivates.why: choosing the sure route to the real goal over a show of strength

commentary.reading: Hanuman's deliberation before speaking to Sita: an envoy must not spoil a task through haste or pride.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 30 in context; plain sense

claim: I will speak good, truthful words of Rama in a gentle voice and arrange it all so that Sita can trust me.

cultivates.why: the opening is designed around a frightened listener
begin with what the other person holds dear

commentary.reading: Hanuman opens by softly reciting Rama's story from the tree so that Sita is not alarmed.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 30 and 31 in context; plain sense

claim: No single means accomplishes even a small task; one who knows many ways to the goal can achieve it.

cultivates.why: keeping more than one route to an aim
resourcefulness in place of one fixed plan

commentary.reading: Hanuman, mission done, reasons about what further can be learned of the enemy's strength before he leaves.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 41 in context; plain sense

claim: Overcome by anger I destroyed the root of a nearly finished task; surely Janaki has perished in the fire I lit.

depicts.why: he sees what his anger did after it is done
terror that he has harmed the one he came to save
the whole mission seems lost by his own hand

commentary.reading: Hanuman's self-reproach after burning Lanka; he then reasons that fire cannot burn Sita, hears she is safe, and sees her again before leaving.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 55 in context; plain sense

line_issue: 'I won a small fight' misreads the first half, which says the task was all but done. Suggested: 'The work was almost finished, and carried away by anger I destroyed its very root.'

claim: An angry person cannot tell what may be said from what may not; for the angry nothing is undoable or unsayable.

heals.why: shows exactly what anger removes: the sense of limits

cultivates.why: knowing in advance what anger will switch off

commentary.reading: Part of Hanuman's reflection on his own anger: a furious person may kill elders and insult the good.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 55 in context; plain sense

claim: The other ministers have held back; I must tell you what I have seen and heard; weigh it and act.

heals.why: he speaks though everyone else has chosen silence

cultivates.why: saying the needed thing to someone powerful

commentary.reading: Vibhishana reports the ill omens in Lanka and urges Sita's return; honest counsel given privately and respectfully first.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 10 in context; plain sense

claim: No one has ever known only victory in battle; a warrior either falls to others or fells them.

heals.why: defeat is shown as part of every contest
one who fell fighting is not to be pitied

cultivates.why: winning and falling held as two sides of entering the field

commentary.reading: Rama consoles Vibhishana: Ravana died as a warrior and such a death is not mourned by the wise.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 109 in context; plain sense

claim: Enmity ends with death and our purpose is done; perform his rites, for he is now mine as he is yours.

heals.why: the quarrel is declared over once it can no longer be fought

cultivates.why: the fallen enemy is given his due
he is claimed as one's own at the end

commentary.reading: Maranantani vairani: Rama asks Vibhishana to cremate Ravana with honour. The enmity ends after the wrong has been stopped, not before.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 109 in context; plain sense

claim: If after growing up and living together you still have not known me, then I am lost forever.

depicts.why: doubted by the one person who should know her best
to be unknown by one's own is the deepest aloneness

commentary.reading: Sita answers Rama's harsh public words with dignity and reproach; she tells him he speaks like a common man to a common woman. Use her protest; do not present the ordeal as a model.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 116 in context; plain sense

claim: I speak not to argue, compete, show superiority or serve my wishes, but truthfully, out of regard for you.

heals.why: four self-serving motives for speaking are named and set aside

cultivates.why: checking why one is about to speak

commentary.reading: Hanuman prefaces his advice on Vibhishana in Rama's council; counsel offered without rivalry toward the other ministers.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 17 in context; plain sense

claim: I would never abandon one who has come in friendship, even if he has faults; the good find no blame in this.

heals.why: one who arrives with faults is still received

cultivates.why: friendship offered is honoured before suspicion
the newcomer is made safe

commentary.reading: Rama overrules his council's suspicion of Vibhishana; a key text for sharanagati in the Srivaishnava reading, where the Lord accepts the seeker faults and all.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 18; Srivaishnava emphasis recalled, not verified in Govindaraja

claim: I am able to build a bridge over the ocean, so let the work begin this very day.

heals.why: he states his ability plainly once the need is clear

cultivates.why: start today
owning a skill he had kept quiet about

commentary.reading: Nala, Vishvakarma's son, speaks up only when the ocean names him; he says one should not praise oneself unasked.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 22 in context; plain sense

claim: Tell me whatever is being said or decided there; that would be the greatest kindness to me.

depicts.why: a captive asks only to know what is being decided about her fate

commentary.reading: Sita asks the kindly Sarama to learn Ravana's intent; Sarama goes and reports back.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 34 in context; plain sense

line_issue: 'Not knowing is the hardest part' is added; the verse is only the request. Suggested: 'Whatever is said or decided there, tell me all of it. That would be the greatest kindness.'

claim: Go, I know you are worn from battle; rest and return armed, and then you will see my strength.

cultivates.why: strength that will not strike an exhausted opponent
even an enemy is allowed to recover

commentary.reading: Rama spares the disarmed Ravana; it is a warrior's fairness and a warning, not gentle advice to rest.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 59 in context; plain sense

line_issue: 'Come back when you're ready' turns a warrior's challenge into self-care advice. Suggested: 'Go. I know you are worn out. Rest, and come back armed; then you will see my strength.'

claim: From the start this was never thought through; proud of your strength alone, you did not weigh the consequences.

heals.why: pride in strength is shown as what blinded him to consequences

commentary.reading: Kumbhakarna's blunt assessment of Ravana, followed by his loyal decision to fight anyway.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 63 in context; plain sense

claim: I do not grieve for my own body as much as for the slander the people have spread.

depicts.why: what hurts most is the false thing said about her
she is abandoned and still thinks of the injustice, not her comfort

commentary.reading: Sita's message through Lakshmana at the forest edge; she is the one wronged and says so with composure.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Uttara Kanda in context; plain sense (the Uttara Kanda's standing is debated by scholars, the commentarial tradition accepts it)

claim: How shall I live in a hermitage, cut off from everyone, and to whom shall I tell my sorrow?

depicts.why: left alone with no one to tell
sorrow is all she has left
she has done nothing to deserve it

commentary.reading: Sita's first words on learning she is to be left in the forest; the grief of someone wronged.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Uttara Kanda in context; plain sense (the Uttara Kanda's standing is debated by scholars, the commentarial tradition accepts it)

claim: Accept this welcome with trust and without distress, as if you had come to your own home; do not despair.

heals.why: an elder says do not despair and offers a place
the abandoned one is given a home

cultivates.why: trust that shelter exists

commentary.reading: Valmiki, knowing her blameless, takes Sita into his ashrama and entrusts her to the women ascetics.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Uttara Kanda in context; plain sense (the Uttara Kanda's standing is debated by scholars, the commentarial tradition accepts it)

claim: For four days I have not attended to the people's work, and it cuts me to the quick.

depicts.why: duty left undone while he was sunk in his own pain

commentary.reading: Rama, after Sita's banishment, reproaches himself for neglecting petitioners and tells the story of King Nriga.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Uttara Kanda in context; plain sense (the Uttara Kanda's standing is debated by scholars, the commentarial tradition accepts it)

claim: The wise should do nothing that harms the people, and good counsel is to be accepted even from the young.

heals.why: an elder changes his plan on a younger brother's word

cultivates.why: advice weighed by its merit, not the speaker's age

commentary.reading: Rama drops the Rajasuya on Bharata's objection that it would bring war on many kings.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Uttara Kanda in context; plain sense (the Uttara Kanda's standing is debated by scholars, the commentarial tradition accepts it)

claim: The tears of the falsely accused destroy the children and herds of a ruler who governs for his own pleasure.

heals.why: the tears of the falsely accused are said to carry weight against those who allowed it

commentary.reading: From the kaccit questions: a king must see that no innocent person is punished.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the kaccit sarga (Ayodhya 100)

claim: Fortunate indeed is Kausalya, whose son will be crowned heir tomorrow.

depicts.why: another's good fortune is counted aloud as one's own loss

commentary.reading: Manthara's words working on Kaikeyi; the voice that feeds comparison, quoted as a warning.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 8 in context; plain sense

claim: Public slander is powerful; knowing her blameless, I abandoned Sita out of fear of the people.

depicts.why: he admits a wrong done knowingly
fear of what people say drove the act

commentary.reading: Rama's admission before Valmiki and the assembly. Sita then refuses a second trial and returns to the earth; the admission does not undo the wrong.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Uttara Kanda in context; plain sense (the Uttara Kanda's standing is debated by scholars, the commentarial tradition accepts it)

claim: Calm, forbearance, straightforwardness and gentle speech are taken for weakness by those without virtue.

depicts.why: patience was offered and treated as incapacity

heals.why: being ignored reflects the other's lack, not one's own

commentary.reading: Rama after three days of humble asking at the shore. Whole arc: humility first, firmness after, and when the ocean appears he listens and redirects the arrow.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 21 in context; plain sense

claim: Because I am forbearing the ocean thinks me incapable; gentle means have failed, so bring my bow.

depicts.why: the moment patience recognises it is being used

cultivates.why: firmness taken up only after gentleness was tried in full

commentary.reading: The turn from sama to danda. It must be read with the three days before and the restraint after; alone it reads as licence for anger.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 21 in context; plain sense

claim: The cool moon will embrace your blameless son like a father as he sleeps, and gladden him.

heals.why: a mother's worry about where her child sleeps is given a tender picture
care still reaches him where she cannot

commentary.reading: Sumitra's consolation of Kausalya: nature itself will tend Rama in the forest.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 44 in context; plain sense

claim: Even the mighty sun and moon, the eyes of the world, undergo eclipse.

heals.why: the greatest lights also go dark for a time
being overtaken by trouble is no mark of smallness

cultivates.why: eclipses pass

commentary.reading: One of Lakshmana's examples to Rama that misfortune reaches even the great.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Aranya 66 in context; plain sense

claim: Your understanding is beyond even the gods; grief has only put your knowledge to sleep, and I am waking it.

heals.why: grief is treated as a sleep over wisdom, not its loss
he is told he is not broken

cultivates.why: his own judgement is called back
the reminder comes with respect

commentary.reading: Lakshmana, the younger, declines to lecture Rama: he only reminds him of what he already knows, then urges effort to find the abductor.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Aranya 66 in context; plain sense

claim: Relieved by hearing of Rama and grieved equally by his grief, Sita was like an autumn night with a half-clouded moon.

depicts.why: relief and sorrow held in the same moment

commentary.reading: Valmiki's image for mixed feeling: the news that he lives lifts her, the news that he suffers weighs on her.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 36 in context; plain sense

claim: Show me your compassion; though I have you as my protector, I appear like one who has no one.

depicts.why: she has someone and still lives as if she had no one
she has to ask to be remembered

commentary.reading: Sita's message to Rama through Hanuman. Devotional readers also hear the soul's plea to its Lord.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 38 in context; devotional reading recalled, not verified

claim: For one as unlucky as I am, your nearness would free me from this great sorrow, if only for a moment.

depicts.why: she asks the one friendly presence to stay a little longer
a moment's relief is all she hopes for

commentary.reading: Sita asks Hanuman to rest a day in hiding before he goes, so her sorrow may lift for a while.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 39 in context; plain sense

claim: Take heart and await the time; before long you will see Rama, blazing like fire.

heals.why: a messenger's assurance that help is already moving
the separation is given an end

cultivates.why: holding on for a named reason
trust in one who is coming

commentary.reading: Hanuman's parting assurance; he leaves at once to bring Rama, so the waiting he asks for is backed by action.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Sundara 39 in context; plain sense

claim: Contain your grief in your heart, mother, and do not sorrow; I will return once I have kept my father's word.

heals.why: a child promises return and asks the parent to bear the interval
the separation has a term

commentary.reading: Rama to Kausalya before leaving; sandharyatam asks her to hold the grief in check.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 21 in context; plain sense

line_issue: 'Hold your sorrow gently' softens sandharyatam, which means restrain or contain. Suggested: 'Keep your sorrow steady in your heart, mother. I will keep my father's word and come home to you.'

claim: Be gracious to me; I cannot go on living far away, like a calf without its mother.

depicts.why: years of duty far from home, and he asks not to be sent away again

commentary.reading: Shatrughna returns from twelve years at Madhura and begs to stay near Rama.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Uttara Kanda in context; plain sense (the Uttara Kanda's standing is debated by scholars, the commentarial tradition accepts it)

claim: You are dearer to me than life, yet the kingdom must be cared for; stay seven nights with me, then return.

heals.why: the longing is met with love and a real visit

cultivates.why: duty is kept without denying the bond

commentary.reading: Rama embraces Shatrughna, affirms the bond, and still asks him to return to his charge after a week.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Uttara Kanda in context; plain sense (the Uttara Kanda's standing is debated by scholars, the commentarial tradition accepts it)

claim: May the dharma you guard with love and discipline guard you in turn.

cultivates.why: trust that a life of right conduct protects
a mother's blessing to carry into hardship

commentary.reading: Kausalya's blessing at Rama's departure; dharmo rakshati rakshitah in the form of a mother's prayer.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Ayodhya 25 in context; plain sense

claim: An enemy who seeks refuge, whether distressed or proud, must be protected by the self-possessed even at the cost of life.

cultivates.why: shelter owed even to a former enemy
being a refuge for the frightened

commentary.reading: Rama cites the sage Kandu's gatha on sharanagata-raksha as he decides to accept Vibhishana.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 18 in context; plain sense

claim: A dove received even the one who took its mate when he came for shelter; how much more should one like me.

cultivates.why: hospitality to one who has done harm
the dove's example set as the least standard

commentary.reading: Rama's example for protecting the refugee; it describes the protector's duty, not a duty on the injured to host those who hurt them.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 18 in context; plain sense

claim: Rama comforted him with words and seemed to drink him in with his eyes.

heals.why: the one who came in fear is looked at with full welcome

cultivates.why: comfort in both word and gaze

commentary.reading: Rama's reception of Vibhishana; devotional readers take it as the Lord's delight in the one who surrenders.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Yuddha 19; devotional reading recalled

claim: Remember me always with great affection, and go free of distress.

cultivates.why: a parting that asks only to be remembered with love

commentary.reading: Rama's farewell to Vibhishana and Sugriva after the coronation.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Uttara Kanda in context; plain sense (the Uttara Kanda's standing is debated by scholars, the commentarial tradition accepts it)

claim: Hearing the nectar of your deeds, I will dispel my longing for you as wind scatters a bank of cloud.

depicts.why: longing for the Lord's presence

heals.why: listening to his story is the remedy named

cultivates.why: a life arranged around hearing of Rama

commentary.reading: Hanuman's boon: to live as long as Rama's story is told and to hear it always; the root of katha-shravana as practice.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Uttara Kanda in context; plain sense (the Uttara Kanda's standing is debated by scholars, the commentarial tradition accepts it)

claim: For each service I would give my life; may I never have to repay you, since repayment needs your trouble.

cultivates.why: a debt gladly left unpaid because paying it would need the friend's misfortune

commentary.reading: Rama's reply to Hanuman: he remains in his debt and wishes Hanuman never needs repaying.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Uttara Kanda in context; plain sense (the Uttara Kanda's standing is debated by scholars, the commentarial tradition accepts it)

claim: The flowers they offered in worship here have still not withered.

heals.why: the teachers are gone and what they offered remains fresh

cultivates.why: sincere offering outlasts the one who made it
a student still tending her teachers' place

commentary.reading: Shabari shows Rama Matanga's grove, where the sages' offerings remain unfaded by the power of their tapas.
commentary.source: Valmiki, Aranya 74 in context; plain sense

claim: As a bird flies on two wings, the highest state is reached through knowledge and action together.

heals.why: the choice between acting and understanding is dissolved
neither duty nor insight has to be dropped

cultivates.why: seeing the two as one flight

commentary.reading: Agastya's answer to Sutikshna in the frame story: jnana and karma together. Advaita readers take action as the purifier that readies the mind for knowledge.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the opening frame; the Advaita qualification is the general traditional position, not a checked gloss

claim: Ever since Rama returned from his pilgrimage he has been low in spirit.

depicts.why: a change others notice before he can explain it

commentary.reading: The attendants' report that opens Rama's vairagya; the tradition treats this dejection as the dawn of discrimination, not illness.
commentary.source: Plain sense within the Vairagya Prakarana; Ananda Bodhendra's Tatparya Prakasha not consulted

claim: He does not brighten at jokes, sink into pleasures or stay with his duties; he only keeps silent.

depicts.why: nothing delights, nothing holds, and he has gone quiet

commentary.reading: Description of Rama's withdrawal before he speaks; Vasishtha and Vishvamitra call it viveka-born vairagya and answer it with teaching.
commentary.source: Plain sense within the Vairagya Prakarana; Ananda Bodhendra's Tatparya Prakasha not consulted

claim: What is kingship or pleasure to me? Who am I, and what is this that has come about?

depicts.why: success and pleasure have stopped answering him
the weariness turns into the question who am I

commentary.reading: The opening of Rama's lament; his question 'ko'ham' is the proper beginning of enquiry, which Vasishtha's teaching then answers.
commentary.source: Plain sense within the Vairagya Prakarana; Ananda Bodhendra's Tatparya Prakasha not consulted

claim: My heart is packed with the stones of sorrow, yet I do not weep, out of fear of my own people.

depicts.why: a heart heavy as stone
tears held back for fear of what family will think

commentary.reading: Rama admits hidden sorrow to the sages; saying it aloud to the teacher is the first step of the cure.
commentary.source: Plain sense within the Vairagya Prakarana; Ananda Bodhendra's Tatparya Prakasha not consulted

claim: People stay gentle with their own and with strangers only until wealth hardens them.

heals.why: shows what prosperity does to tenderness

commentary.reading: From Rama's censure of Lakshmi (wealth): fortune coarsens character.
commentary.source: Plain sense within the Vairagya Prakarana; Ananda Bodhendra's Tatparya Prakasha not consulted

claim: A wealthy person beyond reproach, a brave one who does not boast, and a ruler who sees all alike are rare.

heals.why: success without arrogance is named as the rare achievement

cultivates.why: power joined to even regard
courage without display

commentary.reading: Within the censure of wealth: the three rare men show what fortune usually spoils.
commentary.source: Plain sense within the Vairagya Prakarana; Ananda Bodhendra's Tatparya Prakasha not consulted

claim: That alone is called living by which what is worth attaining is attained and one grieves no more.

heals.why: the emptiness is given a direction: a life aimed at lasting peace

cultivates.why: asking what is truly worth reaching
a measure for a life

commentary.reading: Rama's censure of mere lifespan: life has worth only as the means to the highest repose, nirvriti.
commentary.source: Plain sense within the Vairagya Prakarana; Ananda Bodhendra's Tatparya Prakasha not consulted

claim: The mind is never filled within, even by great riches, like a wicker basket dipped in water.

depicts.why: getting more and still not feeling full

heals.why: the lack is located in the mind, not in the amount

commentary.reading: From Rama's description of chitta: its nature is to remain unfilled.
commentary.source: Plain sense within the Vairagya Prakarana; Ananda Bodhendra's Tatparya Prakasha not consulted

claim: The mind swoops on tasks like a bird on meat and a moment later drops them like a child's toy.

depicts.why: keen starts and instant loss of interest

commentary.reading: Rama on the fickleness of chitta.
commentary.source: Plain sense within the Vairagya Prakarana; Ananda Bodhendra's Tatparya Prakasha not consulted

claim: The mind is the cause of things; the world exists and fades with it, so it must be treated with effort.

heals.why: the place to work is named: the mind itself

cultivates.why: attention turns from circumstances to the mind that meets them

commentary.reading: A seed of the text's central doctrine, voiced by Rama: the world as experienced depends on chitta; the mind is the patient to be treated.
commentary.source: Plain sense within the Vairagya Prakarana; Ananda Bodhendra's Tatparya Prakasha not consulted

claim: Craving, knotted within and hard to cut, drags a person along as a rope drags a bullock.

depicts.why: being pulled along by wanting one cannot cut

commentary.reading: From Rama's censure of trishna.
commentary.source: Plain sense within the Vairagya Prakarana; Ananda Bodhendra's Tatparya Prakasha not consulted

claim: People shed all sorrow by giving up brooding; giving up brooding is the remedy for the sickness of craving.

heals.why: brooding is named as the fuel of craving and sorrow
the remedy is to stop feeding it thought

cultivates.why: letting a wanted thing go unrehearsed

commentary.reading: Chinta here is dwelling on desired objects; dropping that dwelling is called the mantra against the cholera of trishna. It does not dismiss practical concern.
